title: Modify Authentication Process: Conditional Access Policies
shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Conditional Access Policies
summary: Conditional access policies are the rules an identity provider applies before it grants a session: they can require a second factor, demand a managed device, restrict source addresses, or refuse sign-ins that look risky. Cloud platforms express the same idea through policy conditions in their identity and access management rules, checking attributes such as the caller address, the request date, or the region and resource involved. Because these rules are configuration rather than code, this sub-technique is administrative: an intruder with enough rights edits the policy, adds a trusted address range that covers their own host, removes a multi-factor requirement, or permits sign-ins from a region the organisation never uses. The changed policy then makes later access look compliant, so each subsequent sign-in satisfies the rules as written and may raise no alert at all. The evidence is in the identity provider audit trail, which records policy creation, update and deletion events with the acting principal, together with the resulting change in sign-in evaluation. Benign tuning is usually broad or documented, while malicious edits tend to be narrow, recent, and aligned with an account showing odd sign-in behaviour.

beginner.definition: A conditional access policy is a rule that decides whether a sign-in is allowed. It can require a second factor, a company device, or a trusted location. This technique means an attacker changes those rules so that they can get in.
beginner.whyItMatters: These rules exist to stop a stolen password from being enough on its own. If an attacker can edit them, every later sign-in looks acceptable to the system that checks it. Policy changes use normal administration tools, so they often raise no alarm at all. The attacker then keeps access even when the affected passwords are reset.
howItWorks: Before allowing a sign-in, the identity service checks a set of rules about the request.
The rules may require a second factor, a managed device, or a trusted network.
Cloud platforms use similar conditions in their permission policies, such as source address.
An attacker with administration rights edits a rule instead of trying to break it.
They might add their own address range or remove the second factor requirement.
Later sign-ins then satisfy the weakened rule and attract no attention at all.
beginner.example: Imagine a club where the doorman follows a printed list of rules. Members must show a card and a second form of identification. Somebody rewrites one line of that list, so a particular street now counts as inside the club. The doorman keeps checking cards as usual and behaves exactly as trained. Anyone arriving from that street walks straight in. Only a careful reading of the printed list shows that anything changed.
takeaways: Treat conditional access policy edits as security-sensitive changes that need review.
Alert when multi-factor requirements are removed or new trusted ranges appear.
Keep an approved policy baseline so that drift is easy to spot.

objectives: Explain what conditional access policies check before granting access.
Describe how adding trusted ranges or removing requirements weakens protection.
Identify the audit events that record policy changes and the acting identity.
Explain why sign-ins made after the change can look fully compliant.
Recommend review and approval controls for identity policy changes.
